names.name: daughters of Jerusalem
names.gloss: A group of women of the city whom the woman addresses throughout the Song.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: A nomadic Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael, known for its black goat-hair tents.

names.name: En Gedi
names.gloss: A spring-fed oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, famous for vineyards and spices.

insights.title: The Song of songs
insights.body: Song of songs (1:1) is a Hebrew superlative, the best of all songs, like holy of holies. It is one of the five scrolls (Megillot) read at Jewish festivals, and is read at Passover. Rabbi Akiva famously said that all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies.

insights.title: A woman speaks first
insights.body: The Song opens with a woman's desire: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" (1:2). She speaks more lines than anyone else in the book, which is unusual in ancient literature. The labels in WEB, such as Beloved and Friends, are not in the Hebrew; translators infer speakers from the gender of Hebrew words.

insights.title: Dark, but lovely
insights.body: "I am dark, but lovely" (1:5); the Hebrew joining word can mean but or and. She explains that the sun has scorched her because her brothers made her work the vineyards (1:6). Pale skin marked those who did not labour outdoors, so the comment is about work and status. Kedar's tents were woven from black goat hair.

insights.title: A mare among chariots
insights.body: The man compares her to a steed among Pharaoh's chariots (1:9); the Hebrew word is feminine, a mare. Egyptian chariot teams were stallions, and a mare among them would throw the whole force into confusion. It is a compliment to her beauty's power, not to her looks as a horse.

insights.title: Myrrh and henna
insights.body: She calls him a sachet of myrrh between her breasts and a cluster of henna blossoms from En Gedi (1:13-14). Myrrh was a costly imported resin, and henna bushes with fragrant flowers grew at the warm oasis of En Gedi by the Dead Sea.

insights.title: Reading the Song as allegory
insights.body: For centuries Jewish interpreters read the Song as the love between God and Israel, and Christians from Origen onward read it of Christ and the church or the soul. Bernard of Clairvaux preached 86 sermons on it and reached only the start of chapter 3. The prophets already pictured God's covenant as a marriage.

insights.title: Mutual praise
insights.body: "Behold, you are beautiful, my love" (1:15), he says, and she answers, "Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved" (1:16). Their love is expressed in matching words. Their couch is green and the beams of their house are cedars (1:16-17); their meeting place may be outdoors, under the trees.

insights.title: My own vineyard
insights.body: "I haven't kept my own vineyard" (1:6). The vineyard is probably an image for herself, her body and life, as it is later in the Song. What does it suggest that she begins by speaking of a self she has not been free to tend?

1.summary: A young woman longs for her beloved's kisses, explains to the women of Jerusalem why her skin is dark from working in the vineyards, and the two lovers trade praises of each other's beauty.
1.lookfor: Notice who speaks first, the changes between the woman, the man and a group of friends, and the many images of wine, perfume and nature.

names.name: Sharon
names.gloss: The fertile coastal plain of Israel south of Mount Carmel.

names.name: Bether
names.gloss: An unknown place, possibly meaning a cleft or divided mountain.

insights.title: The rose of Sharon
insights.body: "I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys" (2:1). The flower is probably not a rose but a crocus, asphodel or another common wildflower of the coastal plain. She calls herself an ordinary flower; he replies that she is a lily among thorns (2:2).

insights.title: His banner over me
insights.body: He brought me to the banquet hall, literally the house of wine, and his banner over me is love (2:4). A banner marked a military unit or a claim of ownership. His love is displayed openly over her.

insights.title: Raisins and apples
insights.body: Strengthen me with raisins, refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love (2:5). Raisin cakes were festive food. The apple, perhaps an apricot, appears often in the Song as a sign of love and delight.

insights.title: Do not awaken love
insights.body: The refrain "that you not stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires" (2:7) returns in 3:5 and 8:4. Love has its own timing and must not be forced. The oath by gazelles and hinds of the field may play on the sound of two names of God, tsva'ot (of Armies) and El Shaddai, avoiding the divine name while echoing it.

insights.title: Spring in Israel
insights.body: The winter is past, the rain is over, flowers appear, the turtledove is heard and the fig tree ripens (2:11-13). The rainy season in Israel ends in spring, and the turtledove is a migrating bird whose return marks the season. This is part of why Jews read the Song at Passover.

insights.title: Little foxes
insights.body: Catch the little foxes that spoil the vineyards in blossom (2:15). Foxes and jackals damaged vines. In the poem they probably stand for whatever threatens the young love, and the verse has long been applied to small faults that spoil relationships.

insights.title: Mine and his
insights.body: "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (2:16). The same thought returns twice, in reverse order (6:3) and then simply as I am my beloved's (7:10). The Song's love is mutual and exclusive. The prophets used the same language for God and his people: you shall be my people, and I will be your God.

insights.title: Come away
insights.body: He calls through the lattice, Rise up, my love, and come away (2:10). Many Christian readers have heard here Christ's call to the soul. What is gained, and what might be lost, when such a scene is read first as human love?

2.summary: The lovers praise each other with images of flowers and trees, the woman tells of being brought to the banquet hall, and the man invites her to come away with him in springtime.
2.lookfor: Watch for the refrain to the daughters of Jerusalem, the signs of spring, and the little foxes in the vineyards.

names.name: daughters of Zion
names.gloss: Another name for the women of Jerusalem, called to see the king's wedding.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountain range north of Israel, famous for its cedar trees.

insights.title: Him whom my soul loves
insights.body: The phrase him whom my soul loves appears four times in four verses (3:1-4). Her search moves from her bed to the streets and squares and back again. Many think it describes a dream or a longing, since a young woman searching the city at night would have been unusual.

insights.title: My mother's house
insights.body: She brings him into her mother's house (3:4). The phrase appears elsewhere in Ruth and Genesis in matters of marriage. The household of the mother may have been where marriages were planned and celebrated.

insights.title: Up from the wilderness
insights.body: "Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke?" (3:6). The same question returns in 8:5. Pillars of smoke from incense may also recall Israel's journey through the wilderness behind the pillar of cloud, which Jewish interpreters took up in reading the Song as Israel's story.

insights.title: Solomon's carriage
insights.body: The word for carriage in 3:9, appiryon, appears only here in the Bible. It may come from a Greek word for a litter or from Persian, and it describes a portable couch carried on poles. It is built of cedar from Lebanon, with silver, gold and purple (3:10).

insights.title: Sixty mighty men
insights.body: Sixty armed warriors guard the carriage against fear in the night (3:7-8). Wedding parties travelling through open country could be targets for bandits. David's famous mighty men numbered thirty; Solomon's guard is double.

insights.title: A wedding crown
insights.body: Solomon wears the crown his mother gave him on his wedding day (3:11). Bridegrooms wore crowns or garlands at Jewish weddings, a custom the Mishnah says was given up after the war with Rome. Bathsheba's role in making Solomon king adds interest to this detail.

insights.title: A royal wedding
insights.body: Psalm 45 is another royal wedding song in the Bible. The New Testament draws on wedding imagery for Christ as bridegroom and the church as bride. The Song's royal procession has often been read in that light.

insights.title: Night and searching
insights.body: Twice in the Song the woman searches for her beloved at night (3:1-4, 5:6-8). The first time she finds him; the second time she is hurt. Why might the poem include these scenes of absence and longing alongside its scenes of delight? |

3.summary: The woman searches the city at night for the one her soul loves and brings him to her mother's house, and then a splendid royal procession brings King Solomon on his wedding day.
3.lookfor: Notice the repeated phrase him whom my soul loves, the watchmen, and the details of Solomon's carriage and crown.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: Hill country east of the Jordan known for its flocks.

names.name: Amana
names.gloss: A peak in the Anti-Lebanon range north of Israel.

names.name: Senir
names.gloss: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon.

names.name: Hermon
names.gloss: The highest mountain near Israel, snow-capped for much of the year.

insights.title: A praise song of the body
insights.body: Verses 1 to 7 are a type of poem scholars call a wasf, an Arabic term for a poem praising the beloved's body part by part, which was observed in 19th-century Syrian wedding songs. The images are surprising to modern ears but drawn from the familiar world: goats, ewes, a pomegranate, a tower.

insights.title: Goats and ewes
insights.body: Her hair is like a flock of goats descending Mount Gilead (4:1), the dark wavy movement of black goats flowing down a hillside. Her teeth are like freshly washed ewes, each with twins and none missing (4:2): white, even and complete.

insights.title: David's tower
insights.body: Her neck is like David's tower, with a thousand shields hanging on it (4:4). Cities hung shields on their towers and walls as decoration and display, as Ezekiel describes at Tyre. The image is of a neck adorned with necklaces, upright and proud.

insights.title: No spot in you
insights.body: "You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you" (4:7). Paul writes that Christ will present the church to himself without spot or wrinkle. Christian readers have often linked the two passages.

insights.title: Sister and bride
insights.body: He calls her my sister, my bride (4:9-10). In ancient Egyptian love poetry, sister and brother were common terms for lovers. It speaks of closeness and belonging, not literal family.

insights.title: A locked garden
insights.body: She is a locked garden, a sealed fountain (4:12). The images speak of exclusive love reserved for one person, as Proverbs speaks of drinking from one's own well. In 4:13 the word for orchard is pardes, the Persian word behind paradise.

insights.title: Spices from afar
insights.body: Nard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, myrrh and aloes (4:13-14) were mostly costly imports from Arabia, Africa and as far as India. Nard, the same ointment Mary poured on Jesus, came from the Himalayas. The list pictures a garden of every rare delight.

insights.title: Back in the garden
insights.body: The chapter ends with her answer: let the winds blow on my garden and let my beloved come into his garden (4:16). The garden she calls hers becomes his by her free invitation. Many readers see the Song's gardens as a return to Eden, where the man and woman were naked and not ashamed.

4.summary: The man describes his bride's beauty from her eyes to her breasts, calls her from the mountains of Lebanon, and pictures her as a locked garden full of spices, which she then invites him to enter.
4.lookfor: Watch for the order in which he describes her, the many place names, and the shift from a locked garden to an open invitation at the end.

insights.title: The centre of the Song
insights.body: "I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride" (5:1) answers her invitation at the end of chapter 4. By most counts of its lines this is close to the exact middle of the Song. A voice blesses the lovers: Eat, friends! Drink abundantly (5:1). Many read this as the consummation of the marriage.

insights.title: Asleep, but awake
insights.body: "I was asleep, but my heart was awake" (5:2) sets a dreamlike tone. He knocks with his hair wet with dew, and she hesitates because she has already undressed and washed her feet (5:3). When she finally opens, he is gone (5:6).

insights.title: Myrrh on the lock
insights.body: Her hands drip with myrrh on the handles of the lock (5:5). Doors were secured with a wooden bolt that could be reached through a hole. The detail may mean he left perfume as a token, or that she had prepared herself for him.

insights.title: Beaten by the watchmen
insights.body: The watchmen who earlier helped her search (3:3) now beat her and take her cloak (5:7). The scene is painful and unexplained. Some take it as a nightmare, others as the real dangers a woman faced alone at night. The poem does not soften it.

insights.title: Better than another?
insights.body: The daughters of Jerusalem ask what makes her beloved better than any other (5:9). Her answer is the only full praise of the man's body in the Song (5:10-16). He is white and ruddy, the best among ten thousand.

insights.title: Gold, ivory and marble
insights.body: His head is gold, his body ivory set with sapphires, his legs pillars of marble on gold bases (5:11-15). The description sounds like a precious statue, a masterpiece of the finest materials. Ivory was a luxury import, as Solomon's ships show.

insights.title: Altogether lovely
insights.body: He is altogether lovely; this is my beloved, and this is my friend (5:16). Christian hymns and devotion have often applied the words altogether lovely to Christ. In the poem itself she ends by naming him her friend as well as her beloved.

insights.title: Too late to open
insights.body: She delays, and when she opens he is gone (5:6). What does the scene suggest about the risk of hesitation in love, human or divine?

5.summary: The man enters his garden and friends bless the lovers, then the woman hesitates when he knocks at night, finds him gone, is beaten by the watchmen, and describes his beauty to the daughters of Jerusalem.
5.lookfor: Notice the midpoint of the Song at the first verse, how the second night search differs from the first, and the only full description of the man's body.

names.name: Tirzah
names.gloss: An early capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, whose name means pleasing.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: Hill country east of the Jordan known for its flocks.

names.name: Shulammite
names.gloss: The woman's only title in the Song, of uncertain meaning.

names.name: Mahanaim
names.gloss: A town east of the Jordan whose name means two camps.

insights.title: I am my beloved's
insights.body: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" (6:3) reverses the order of 2:16. After the pain of chapter 5, she knows where he is and to whom he belongs. The search ends not with finding him in the streets but in knowing they belong to each other.

insights.title: As Tirzah, as Jerusalem
insights.body: She is beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem (6:4). Tirzah was the capital of the northern kingdom until Omri moved it to Samaria in the 9th century BC. Pairing it with Jerusalem compares her to the most splendid cities. Some scholars think the mention of Tirzah points to an early date for this poem.

insights.title: Awesome as an army
insights.body: She is awesome as an army with banners (6:4, 6:10). The word awesome, ayom, is usually used of terrifying things. Her beauty overwhelms him, so that he asks her to turn her eyes away (6:5).

insights.title: Sixty queens
insights.body: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, but his dove is unique (6:8-9). The numbers are modest beside Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines in Kings. Even the queens praise her. Love sees one person as beyond comparison.

insights.title: Moon and sun
insights.body: She looks out as the morning, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun (6:10). The words used are poetic: levanah, the white one, for moon, and chammah, the hot one, for sun. She is pictured with the splendour of the heavens.

insights.title: A puzzling verse
insights.body: Verse 12 is among the hardest in the Song to translate; the Hebrew may mean my desire set me among the chariots of my noble people, or contain a name, Amminadib. Translations vary widely, and no reading is certain. |

insights.title: The Shulammite
insights.body: She is called the Shulammite (6:13), the only name or title she is given. It may be a feminine form of Solomon, the Solomon-woman, or link her to Shunem, home of the beautiful Abishag in David's last days. The dance of Mahanaim, two camps, may be a dance between two rows of onlookers.

insights.title: Verse numbers differ
insights.body: In WEB and most English Bibles, 6:13 is verse 7:1 in the Hebrew Bible, so all the verses of chapter 7 are one number higher in Hebrew. Readers comparing translations or commentaries should watch for this.

6.summary: The woman says her beloved has gone to his garden and declares that they belong to each other, and the man praises her as awe-inspiring and unique among all queens, before the friends call her back to dance.
6.lookfor: Look for the city names in the man's praise, the comparison with queens and concubines, and the first time the woman is given a name.

names.name: Heshbon
names.gloss: An ancient city east of the Jordan, known for its pools.

names.name: Bathrabbim
names.gloss: A gate of Heshbon, its name meaning daughter of many.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: The capital of Aram (Syria), north-east of Israel.

names.name: Carmel
names.gloss: A wooded mountain on Israel's coast.

insights.title: From feet to head
insights.body: This praise song begins with her feet in sandals and moves upward to her head (7:1-5), the reverse of chapter 4. It may describe her dancing, following the call to gaze at the Shulammite. The images become more intimate and bolder.

insights.title: Pools of Heshbon
insights.body: Her eyes are like the pools of Heshbon (7:4). Excavations at Tell Hesban in Jordan found a large reservoir from the Iron Age. Her nose like the tower of Lebanon facing Damascus and her head like Carmel compare her to the grandest landmarks.

insights.title: Hair like purple
insights.body: The hair of her head is like purple, and the king is held captive in its tresses (7:5). Purple dye from sea snails was the most expensive dye in the ancient world and a sign of royalty. Her hair is dark and glossy, and holds the king captive.

insights.title: The palm tree
insights.body: Her stature is like a palm tree, and he will climb it to take hold of its fruit (7:7-8). Date palms were climbed to harvest their fruit. The name Tamar, borne by several women in the Bible, means palm.

insights.title: His desire is toward me
insights.body: "I am my beloved's. His desire is toward me" (7:10). The word for desire, teshuqah, appears only three times in the Bible. In Genesis 3 the woman's desire is for her husband, who will rule over her, a result of the fall. Here the desire runs from him to her, and there is no ruling, which many read as love restored.

insights.title: Mandrakes
insights.body: The mandrakes produce fragrance (7:13). The mandrake root was believed to promote love and fertility, as when Rachel bargained with Leah for them. The Hebrew dudaim sounds like dodim, love.

insights.title: Out into the fields
insights.body: She invites him into the fields, villages and vineyards, where she will give him her love (7:11-12). The setting has moved from the court and the city to the countryside. The Song repeatedly places love in nature, in blossom and spring.

insights.title: Delight without shame
insights.body: The Song speaks of the body and desire openly, in a book of Scripture (7:6). What does it suggest about God's view of the body and of desire within love?

7.summary: The man praises the woman's beauty from her feet to her head as she dances, longs to climb the palm tree, and she invites him out into the fields and vineyards where she will give him her love.
7.lookfor: Watch for the direction of the description, the place names used as comparisons, and the woman's statement about desire.

names.name: Baal Hamon
names.gloss: A place otherwise unknown, where Solomon had a large vineyard.

insights.title: If you were my brother
insights.body: She wishes he were like her brother, so she could kiss him in public and no one would despise her (8:1). Open affection was acceptable only between close relatives. Her love must for now remain more private than she wishes.

insights.title: Who is this?
insights.body: "Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?" (8:5) echoes 3:6. This time the couple come together, she leaning on him. The scene under the apple tree where his mother bore him links their love to the generations.

insights.title: Set me as a seal
insights.body: "Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm" (8:6). A seal was worn on a cord around the neck or as a ring, and served as a person's signature. She asks to belong to him so closely that she becomes his identity.

insights.title: A flame of Yahweh
insights.body: Love is strong as death, jealousy as cruel as Sheol, its flashes a very flame of Yahweh (8:6). The Hebrew shalhevetyah may simply mean a mighty flame, but its ending can be read as the divine name. If so, this is the only place in the Song where God is named.

insights.title: Many waters
insights.body: "Many waters can't quench love, neither can floods drown it" (8:7). In the Bible many waters often stand for the chaos only God can master. Paul says that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love.

insights.title: Love cannot be bought
insights.body: If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned (8:7). Love is a gift, not a purchase. The next verses about the little sister's brothers may show how families arranged marriages and bride-prices.

insights.title: Wall or door
insights.body: The brothers ask what to do for their little sister: if she is a wall they will build on her, if a door they will enclose her (8:8-9). The images probably refer to her chastity and readiness for marriage. The woman replies that she is a wall and has found peace in his eyes (8:10).

insights.title: An open ending
insights.body: Solomon has a great vineyard he leases out, but her own vineyard is hers to give (8:11-12), echoing the vineyard she had not kept (1:6). The book ends not with a wedding scene but with her call, Come away, my beloved (8:14), longing still alive. Christians have heard in it the Bible's final cry, Come, Lord Jesus.

8.summary: The woman wishes she could show her love openly, gives the Song's great statement that love is strong as death, and the book ends with her brothers' concern for their little sister, a word about vineyards, and a final call for the beloved to come.
8.lookfor: Look for the seal, the comparison of love with death and fire, and how the Song ends without a neat conclusion.

intro.who: The title links the Song to Solomon (1:1), but the Hebrew can mean by, for or about Solomon, and he appears in the poems mostly as a figure in the background. Jewish and Christian tradition long credited Solomon, who is said to have written over a thousand songs, while most modern scholars see it as anonymous love poetry, perhaps a collection, in which a woman's voice leads.
intro.when: On the traditional view it comes from Solomon's reign in the 10th century BC. Its vocabulary, including a Persian word for orchard (4:13), leads many scholars to date its final form to the Persian or early Greek period, though some of the poems may be much older.
intro.why: It celebrates the love, desire and mutual delight of a woman and a man in rich poetry of gardens, vineyards and spices. Jewish tradition read it as the love between God and Israel and reads it at Passover, and Christians have long read it of Christ and the church or the soul; many readers today take it first as a celebration of human love that also points to God's love.
